claims.statement: The `haap` executable is declared in `[project.scripts]` as `haap = "haap.cli:main"`; `main()` builds one argparse parser whose subcommand handlers are registered with `set_defaults(func=...)` and dispatched by calling `args.func(args)`.

CLI exit conventions: command-level failures print to stdout and return 1 (e.g. `haap init` when an identity already exists); `HAAPError` subclasses raised in handlers are caught by `main()`, printed to stderr as `HAAP error [<code>]: <detail>` and yield exit code 2; a `KeyboardInterrupt` reaching `main()` returns 130, while the `serve` and `registry serve` handlers catch Ctrl+C themselves, stop the server and return 0.

Stores resolve the agent state root as `$HAAP_DIR` falling back to `~/.haap` (`haap_dir()`); each `cmd_*` handler constructs fresh `IdentityStore`/`Directory`/`TaskRegistry`/`AuditLog` per invocation passing the top-level `--dir` value, which overrides the environment variable and, being declared only on the root parser, must appear before the subcommand (e.g. `haap --dir /srv/agent-b friends list`).

`haap init --name --endpoint` generates a fresh Ed25519 identity through `IdentityStore.create(display_name, endpoint_url)` and persists `<dir>/identity.json` atomically with 0600 permissions; running init again against the same directory prints 'identity already exists at ...' and exits 1 because `create()` refuses to overwrite unless `overwrite=True`.

`haap whoami` prints `Identity.public_claims()` as indented JSON — display_name, fingerprint and an endpoint {transport, url} block only when configured — the key-free public projection also used to build manifests; before `haap init` it fails via `NotInitializedError` (exit code 2).

`haap friends add FP --public-key --name --endpoint` only records the peer locally as a `pending_out` entry via `Directory.add_pending_out` (fingerprint, friend's public key, endpoints, conservative default grant template) and performs no network I/O; sending the wire-level `friend_request` is done from Python with `HAAPClient.start_friendship(...)`, which the README documents as the companion step.

`haap friends requests` lists the `pending_in` queue (fingerprint, name, message, declared speciality) and ends each entry with a copy-ready `haap friends approve <fp> --role [...]` command listing the currently available roles, while `haap friends roles` prints one line per available role template (built-ins plus roles.json overrides) with its description and granted action keys.

`haap friends approve FP --role R` is the human approval: it resolves the named role with `resolve_role` and calls `Directory.approve(fp, grant=spec permissions, rate_limits=spec rate_limits)`, transitioning the record from `pending_in` to `accepted` with that template's matrix; `--grant` supplies a raw JSON matrix instead, and approving a fingerprint not in `pending_in` raises `FriendNotFoundError` (exit 2).

CLI friendship approval changes local `friends.json` state only: `cli.py` never sends envelopes, and the only code path that emits a wire `friend_accept` is the server's policy auto-approve branch, so notifying a queued requester of a CLI approval requires embedding integration — flagged on the README roadmap as the unfinished Hermes-webhook bridge.

`haap friends deny FP` rejects an inbound request by deleting the `pending_in` record; `haap friends remove FP` deletes any relationship regardless of status; `haap friends block FP` sets or creates a `blocked` record with an emptied permission matrix, which makes the server reject every future message from that fingerprint (the documented way to stop marketplace abuse).

`haap capabilities [--speciality S] [--show-all]` builds the capability manifest on the fly from `Identity.public_claims()` plus an introspection of installed Hermes skills; by default it prints a one-line summary (fingerprint, name, skills/tools counts) and with `--show-all` the full JSON, but it never writes `capabilities.json` — that optional export (`capabilities.export_manifest`) belongs to embedding code.

`haap task list` reads a file-backed `TaskRegistry` from `tasks.json` filtering by `--role` (delegate|submit) and `--friend`; `haap task send` always raises `HAAPError` directing operators to the Python API, because HAAPServer and HAAPClient default to in-memory TaskRegistries (`memory=True`) so under a stock CLI setup nothing writes tasks.json and the list stays empty until an embedder injects a file-backed registry.

`haap serve --host --port --speciality` (defaults 0.0.0.0:8443) loads the local identity, a file-backed Directory and AuditLog, constructs HAAPServer and starts a ThreadingHTTPServer exposing `POST /haap/messages`, `GET /.well-known/haap.json` and `GET /health`; it blocks until Ctrl+C, then calls `server.stop()` and exits 0.

A stock `haap serve` constructs its own `RequestPolicy` from the data directory's policy.json (read once at server construction, so policy edits require a restart) and defaults its notifier to `ConsoleNotifier`, printing pending-approval cards to stderr; when an inbound request auto-approves, the server resolves the capped role through `resolve_role` — which reloads roles.json on each call — and returns a `friend_accept` carrying the real granted matrix and granted_role.

`haap registry serve` (default 0.0.0.0:8444) runs the in-repo, in-memory RegistryServer with proof-of-endpoint registration, heartbeat renewal and search, and prints its generated directory fingerprint; the README presents it for demos/communities and points production at the standalone `haap-dird` service.

`haap registry register` performs the full signed registration flow (`register()` in registry_client: submit signed manifest, sign the returned challenge nonce as endpoint proof, complete at /register/complete) against `--registry`, using `--endpoint` or the identity's declared endpoint_url and raising `HAAPError` when neither exists; `haap registry search` GETs /search with `--capability`/`--query` and prints matching agents or '(no results)'.

`haap audit [--last N] [--friend FP]` prints the most recent entries (default 30) of the append-only JSON-lines `audit.log` as timestamp, event, friend and result; the log rotates at 5 MB keeping two rotated copies, and sensitive keys (challenge_token, private_key, signature, task_payload) are redacted before writing.

`roles.json` overlays user roles on the built-ins guest/client/partner/family/admin: a role spec may set `extends` to inherit from a built-in (or earlier user role), the extends key is consumed, and other top-level keys replace the base wholesale; a missing, unreadable or invalid-entry file silently falls back to built-ins, and roles.json is re-read on every `resolve_role` call so edits take effect on the next approve or auto-approval without restart.

`policy.json` configures the friend-request engine evaluated in fixed order deny → auto-approve → queue: `default` is queue (the fallback when the file is missing or malformed) or deny; `auto_approve` rules match first-wins on exact fingerprint or case-insensitive speciality; `max_role` caps auto-approvals on the ladder guest < client < partner < family < admin, and unknown/custom role names auto-approve capped at client.

The README's production recipe runs `haap serve` as a systemd unit (`ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/haap serve --port 8443`, `Restart=on-failure`, `WantedBy=multi-user.target`) and advises opening the port in the firewall and terminating HTTPS with a reverse proxy (Caddy/nginx) or tunnel (cloudflared) because the built-in server is plain HTTP.

The pytest suite does not invoke the argparse CLI; CLI-facing semantics are pinned through the underlying libraries: `test_policy.py::test_approve_with_role_template` reproduces the `friends approve --role` path (resolve_role then Directory.approve with the template's permissions and rate limits), policy tests cover roles.json inheritance, max_role capping and queue/auto/deny outcomes, and `test_registry_client.py` exercises the register/search flow behind the registry subcommands.
